utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Please be seated. Today the intention is to have a Status Conference in the truest sense of this word. We'll say to find out what is the status of our case and come back to all the still-open issues. I have three or four pages of bits and pieces to be addressed. And in addition, the intention is, in order to proceed as expeditious as possible, to prepare the admission of additional documents which, of course, can't be done in the framework of a Status Conference. But prepare it by attaching numbers, hearing objections, and then in a package solution, to transfer the decisions of this Status Conference as regards the admission into evidence of documents, yes, as a package into the hearings by the way of just making reference to this Status Conference, and to have the transcripts of this Status Conference as an attachment of tomorrow's hearings. As to the fact that in all likelihood, Judge Fassi Fihri will be not available throughout the entire week, we have to plan how to proceed. My intention is to use the two remaining days under Rule 15 bis, first of all, for the upcoming witness from abroad. And I hope that we can start immediately tomorrow morning with this witness. And I learned, please correct me if I am wrong, that it would be take about two hours to hear this witness. Is this correct? Two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Two days. Wishful thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I hoped that it would finish a bit early, and if so, I would suggest finishing Mr. Sebire, if that happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about the presence of Mr. Ostojic? Will he be here on Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic promised that he will come when necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And when there is a promise, he will no doubt be here. So indeed, that would be an excellent solution, because correct me once again if I'm wrong, Mr. Sebire is prepared to leave the country by the end of the week?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe the 15th or something like that, he is scheduled to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So we should envisage to hear Witness -- what was the number -- 33 tomorrow, and then proceed with Mr. Sebire. And then we have to find out how to proceed. I'll let you know as soon as possible when we can proceed. But we have to take into account worst case, this would be that it takes some other days, maybe even during the next week, before Judge Fassi Fihri is coming back. And my idea would be to continue, nevertheless, with witnesses from abroad, then in the form of taking depositions under Rule 71. I think this would be a feasible method, and this would allow all participants to be present and to cross-examine this witness. But as mentioned, only in case and not to be delayed and to avoid unnecessary expenses for witnesses coming to The Hague from abroad which could be heard then. But it can be discussed later, only that you know what the intention is. But, let me invite you, first of all, some general observations to this envisaged proceedings for the next two or three weeks. Anything by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: As to the schedule, Your Honour, we just would appreciate, if there was any change in the schedule for our next witness from abroad, who I believe is scheduled to testify next Monday, that we be notified as soon as possible because he has a very busy schedule and has blocked off particular days. That's Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Would there be any objections to proceed with this witness under Rule 71, and the Trial Chamber would then appoint one of the permanent Judges, this would be in all likelihood me, myself, as a "presiding officer" for that purpose? And then introduce this into the hearing as foreseen under Rule 71. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections from our side, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There would be no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From the OTP, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't see any at the present time. You just hit me with the idea. I haven't really considered it. But I don't see -- nothing comes to mind. I'm not complaining, but I don't see a reason why we would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Problems when they are upcoming, there's always a way to overcome. And I think Rule 71 would be the most appropriate situation. Today's Status Conference, as you heard, is -- there is no intention at all to discuss substantive law issues or factual issues. The time is ripe for this status after -- by the end of the Prosecutor's case, and indeed, as you can see from the updated schedule, it is still envisaged to discuss in how far it's possible to streamline the case, both as regards the facts whereby the OTP already now it can be said, for whatever reasons so ever, we didn't manage to bring the necessary evidence, and it should be really concentrated, then, on the core issues. The intention of these deliberations, no doubt, is that we once again avoid unnecessary battlefields with long, long files where the parties seem to agree. And this could be as regards facts from the side of the Defence, if I understood the messages from the side of both Dr. Stakic himself when asking, for example, asking for not cross-examining the one or other witnesses which has already been taken into account and is laid down in our files as a real good sign of cooperation, that it would be really helpful that during these hearings, notwithstanding an in-depth discussion on the question whether the link has been established and whether there is a responsibility and, in concreto, a criminal responsibility of Dr. Stakic that we shouldn't discuss questions of the crimes committed in that territory as such. So therefore, already from this factual basis, both the motion under 98 bis and, no doubt, also the answer on this and the decision on this can be abbreviated. And with the same appellate function, we want to discuss the same matters as regards legal issues. Here, we should really concentrate on core issues which, no doubt, as regards genocide, the question of the necessary intent, the core element of crime of this offence, and that we concentrate on other issues, the applicability of, say, the Geneva conventions in the concrete case, vis-a-vis a civil person. And such problems as pointed out already earlier by the Defence. And when I mention this, the basis for this is that I stem from a legal system where it's mandatory to give some judicial hints in order to avoid surprises. And two core issues, if - emphasise "if" - the Trial Chamber would come to the conclusion that with respect to the one or other offence the necessary mens rea has been established during the Prosecutor's case, that we have to discuss whether this is in the scope of foreseeability, the one or other incident, and I have to direct the intention of both parties to two special issues and that is the incidents in Room Number 3. I want to draw the attention, especially of the Defence, to the fact that as regards Room Number 3, it doesn't go without saying that this Chamber comes to the same conclusions another Trial Chamber has come to alia in a previous case because it might be that in this other case, the reason why Room Number 3 has not been included, put it this way, could be more or less based on technical intentions in this special case. So therefore, the evaluation of whether or not there is a responsibility, individual responsibility, as regards the incident in Room Number 3 on both days should be discussed in depth. But the same is true, and this goes in the direction of the Office of the Prosecutor, please take care that it doesn't go without saying that the incidents at Mount Vlasic are immediately within the scope of the foreseeability, and it has to be discussed, without doubt, whether or not there could have been a deviation from, if any, from a criminal plan. So I think these should be the core issues we have to deal with when we have to address 98 bis. And the so-called deliberations, indeed, should facilitate these proceedings, abbreviate the proceedings, and no doubt abbreviate the motions and the decision. And you should never give up the hope, maybe at the end of these deliberations, we could come back once again to the question whether or not the parties couldn't reach an agreement as foreseen in the rules. But it would be premature to discuss these issues in the framework of a Status Conference dedicated to formal issues, first of all. Any observations to this long introduction? I can't see any. So let's leave it with this for today. Let me now start all these bits and pieces. As regards Witness Z, we are still expecting the originals of Exhibits S290, 292, and 293. Of course, this takes time. But in addition, it is necessary that we can introduce or make use of former statements that we know the source -- that we know something more about the sources. We have, for example, from this statement evidently stemming from about 1994, taken somewhere in Germany, we need the original. We can't work with a, yes, with the English version only when we don't have the German one. And in addition, one question remains open: That is, what about the notes? Where do they stem from? What have they to do with Witness Z?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, they have nothing to do with Witness Z in the sense of what we are presenting as evidence to the Court. And there seems to be some confusion. Neither of those statements, none of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the written statements, are offered by the Prosecution as evidence in line with Your Honours' earlier clear rulings that the Court is relying upon the oral evidence of witnesses at trial and not prior statements. The only reason the Court received those is because Your Honour requested them, that anything we give to the Defence we give to the Chamber for review. We are required by the rules to give all prior statements to the Defence. They are not evidence. They are not offered as evidence. And as regards to the German statement, we don't have it in German. We're not offering it in evidence, either the English or the German. So I don't know if there was -- if there was a confusion about what we were giving those to the Chamber for, but we are not giving those statements to the Chamber as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please recall that as regards one very special incident mentioned by Witness Z, that is, whether or not Dr. Stakic at that time wore a uniform or not, reference was made also by the Chamber to this formal statement. To that extent, that it seems to be -- I have to be cautious, it seems to be that already in 1994 Witness Z mentioned this. So it's part of the transcript, and it's part of the hearing of this witness. But it can only be included, especially for the purposes of a judgement, if we have the basis of this, and it should be no problem at all to trace where this document comes from. It can't come out of the blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We know exactly where it came from. We, I believe -- well, I know we would have some record of it. I believe we received it from the commission of experts. But again, we do not have the German statement. We were not offering the statements as evidence. The witness did answer regarding her prior recollections or statements regarding the uniform. But we can't provide something we don't have. Is Your Honour saying that we have to contact the German authorities? It's not part of the evidence that we're presenting. Moreover, the notes that you referred to are notes that are written in English that have not, to our knowledge, been read back to her. We don't know who took those notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. I think, no doubt, we can forget about these notes, but it could be, no doubt, helpful or even mandatory to make use of all, if you would, please, read up once again the transcript of Witness Z, that we can make use of this part when we have these -- the original statement in German as well. So I would ask the OTP to try to find out whether these documents are available or not because I didn't want to make a problem out of this complex in the presence of the witness and in the very limited remaining time. But indeed, it is a problem that such documents are presented more or less out of the blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would Your Honour prefer that we don't present those documents? It's not our intention that they be admitted. She did not have a chance to review or adopt that document. And that's a problem. If we're presenting documents that could have a statement that she could explain in Court at a later time when she hasn't had an opportunity to explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I had the impression that counsel of the OTP, Ms. Sutherland, wanted to explain this at the end of the day, but for the special time limitations, it was already later than 7.00, I didn't want to hear any further explanations. So I hope to obtain an explanation on this today. So I mention it, and I hope that it will be possible to obtain the original. As regards Mr. Sebire, what about a new table? Would this be feasible until Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: He's working on it. He has been working on it all weekend, and we hope it will be ready on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the list, the updated list of missing persons, is it now available, because no doubt it should form part of Column 1 of this table to be expected?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It has not yet been received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about the title for the annexes to this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We have it to distribute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May it be distributed. May I hear the exhibit number of this report, if there is already any, that we can have this as an attachment to this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We believe it's 281.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it confirmed, 281? Then let's mark it provisionally, as mentioned before, we will confirm this in the hearing, during the hearing, as 281-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe we have a -1.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, S281-1 is the annex number 16 already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then let's continue with -2. Please don't tell me already there's a -2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Apparently there's a 2 and a 3. I think we need to make it -4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't have an updated list. Then finally, the Defence asked Mr. Sebire to provide an answer to the question of the 261 gravesites that were exhumed, how many were mass graves and how many were individual graves. Will this also be feasible to identify by tomorrow or by Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure by Wednesday. It's a matter of simply reviewing all 261 because Mr. Sebire indicated he did not have a record of it. But just to clarify the question, is "mass graves" defined as a grave with more than one body?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be honest, I haven't found yet a definition of "mass grave," a mandatory definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think his report, he distinguished between graves with - I could be wrong - but more than five bodies and less --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we should leave the definition for Mr. Sebire, and maybe this word has been used earlier, no doubt, in this Tribunal. And we should stick to former definitions which I can't quote from the top of my head. We shouldn't forget one additional question, and I want to put this today, in order that Mr. Sebire is prepared for these questions: We have numerous reports by United Nations or, for the purposes of United Nations Security Council, for example, prepared by Ms. Greaves in the Prijedor report, and by Professor Cherif Bassiouni. And from this we know that there have been numerous exhumations conducted before and on behalf of the United Nations, on behalf of the International Red Cross, and also by and on behalf of nongovernmental examinations. As far as I understood, Mr. Sebire's report, he is making reference only to those reports -- exhumations conducted by official authorities in the entities or in Croatia or in Yugoslavia, but not to these United Nations, NGO, or International Red Cross based exhumations. What about this? Have they been included? Will they be included? Have they been taken into account?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm not aware of NGO exhumations in the area of Prijedor. They may have funded the state authorities, or provided assistance. But Mr. Sebire is the expert. He can tell us. I don't believe they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: He can assist us in this. And if there was no such exhumation in the area of Prijedor, he may let us know. But please recall that he mentioned also that there were exhumations conducted related to Prijedor but not in the municipality of Prijedor. Therefore, we should take these exhumations mentioned in several United Nations reports, Security Council reports, we should take this into account, not to be confused. As regards Mr. Inayat, the Chamber had asked Mr. Inayat to go through the sourcing for the documents in the Stakic case, ascertain whether any of those from the organisation AID have been allegedly indicted for fraud were connected with the provisional documents to the ICTY. Will this be delivered before we hear Mr. Inayat once again, or what about this? And in addition, there is the request by the Defence to provide the IIF for Exhibit 39, the famous variant A and B document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first, as to Mr. Inayat, my understanding was that he had completed his testimony, so my suggestion is in regards to that question, which the Court put to him and he agreed to answer and I know he is working on that, that he simply provide a 92 statement from him and it will cover that. And he will provide that shortly. And again, the only task that he has been given is to review the documents presented in this case to see which ones, if any, have come from five individuals. As for the IIF, it's not our practice, we don't want to make it a practice, that we give out an internal document like that. In regards to the specific variant A and B, we actually want to provide the Court with much more detailed information, and that is the testimony of Mr. O'Donnell where he went through the -- all of the documents of variant A and B which were obtained by the Tribunal and the source of those documents, if I quote a number, I would be guessing, but I know there's more than seven, I think there's seven or more various copies of this document have been received by the Office of the Prosecutor. It's all contained in the testimony of Mr. O'Donnell who testified in the Bosanski Samac case and was subject to cross-examination on that point. We are in the process of offering his testimony under 92 bis. And the Court is aware that there was a ruling in that case regarding the authenticity of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. I think the Defence is aware of this as well. Finally, the request of the Defence as regards an index of documents received by the OTP from the agency for identification and documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the investigation of the Office of the Prosecutor is not public, and until evidence and documents are presented in court, we don't believe that the Court, Chambers, and Defence should be looking at our documents. The specific documents that we received and presented in this case, we have provided the index to the sourcing document through Mr. Inayat. In fact, we went beyond that in this case, far beyond it, and we provided about 2.000 pages regarding seizures of documents, an index of the seizures of documents, including documents we didn't provide. The Defence never invoked reciprocal discovery. We have given the Defence a lot of documents, and we haven't received one from them. We certainly don't think it's a good practice and we don't intend to give out sources of documents that we have not used and will not use in this case. But we have complied with -- Mr. Inayat has provided in the sourcing an indication of the source of each of the documents that we have presented in this case. If more documents come up that we intend to produce, again, Mr. Inayat will provide the source of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I hear the observations to these points by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to tell the Chamber, actually to Your Honour, that it wasn't 2.000, it was 3.019 pages. We asked to have it in electronic version, but we got it in hard copy so it was pretty hard to handle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the protection of first, the Chamber decided not to request a copy of this. It's not, please correct me, but we don't think that it would be of assistance for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a huge pile of papers, and just index, so I don't think that it would be of any assistance to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what about the other issues mentioned just before?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Regarding AID documents and the providers of these documents, I think that it would be of an immense assistance, both to the Chamber and to the Defence, to see whether those documents were received and obtained from persons allegedly committing the crimes of fraud. And regarding those IIF forms, I think that it can be marked as confidential and then Chamber and the Defence would be able to review them and have access to them. I don't know whether Your Honour wants anything else from the Defence. One more thing, we are not able to follow the transcript because all our monitors are dead. So if possible...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have already asked for this, and the same is true for me. No Livenote. No transcript. I don't know, what about the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We have our monitors working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We could turn it off to make it fair. I don't know if anyone has tried. Ms. Karper has suggested pushing the computer button underneath the desk to turn it on. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No. It's completely dead, and the same is true unfortunately for Livenote. Hopefully it will be available in printed form for us as soon as possible. During this Status Conference, I don't want to make rulings on these issues. But as regards the IIF for Exhibit 39, it would be, indeed, in the interests of justice to know, even if it's under seal, to find out from which source, and as we heard, sources these documents were, indeed, obtained. And it would help if we could identify where documents were found, and to be honest, I'm more than surprised that, for example, we never received, as it would be the state of art, a list of documents found in the former office of Dr. Stakic. So therefore, especially for these purposes, and the burden of proof, especially to establish the necessary link, it would be helpful, especially for this extraordinary important document, to have not as a rule but as an exception in this case at least the information where these documents were found. It would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's extremely reasonable, and, Your Honour, I believe that that has been provided. The IIF form is what Mr. Inayat uses to create his sourcing. So the source of Exhibit 39 is in, I believe, list 1 from Mr. Inayat. And also in the testimony that will be proffered from Mr. O'Donnell, testimony that we intend to offer by 92 bis. There's an extensive discussion of the source of not only this particular copy of the variant A and B but all of the copies, where they were obtained from, and a lot of cross-examination on those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this, indeed, can be of some necessary assistance for the Defence and the Chambers. Just for the transcript, I can see now Livenote being really live and not Deadnote. And also the transcript is working. Also the same is true for the Defence. I see nodding. And Dr. Stakic, you can follow also -- okay, thank you. This was accepted by nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Ms. Karper asked me to clarify for the record that the exhibit that was mentioned as Exhibit 39 is actually numbered SK39 because it came in during Mr. Donia's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. Then, once again, coming back to Mr. Sebire's testimony, normally the rule applies that the Judges know the law, judex novit curia, but as regards law from abroad, this principle is not applicable as you can find it in several international conventions on information of laws from other countries. And on this basis, indeed, it would be not only helpful, but it seems to be mandatory for a better understanding of the column indicating which individuals were named in a court certificate declaring them dead which were and which are the prerequisites under the law in Bosnia and Herzegovina to declare these individuals to be dead. Can we maybe receive this applicable law?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The law in question is the law of administrative procedure beginning in Article 60 of the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina, through Article 73. I have a translation of that, but first let me explain two things: The source of this is actually taken from a book that was published in 1989. So it was the law at the time the book was written of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is the same law that is in effect on this issue today, but I don't have a copy of the statute book. I know that from the judge who has been providing these certificates of death. Our main point was that the Defence, Mr. Ostojic, said that there was a law that required families to make an application for declaration of death. We will submit to Your Honours the sections. There has one revision that has to be done, so I'm not prepared to do that right now, in the translation. Because the translator erroneously translated SRBH as Serbian Republic, as opposed to Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But it's our position that -- it's very difficult to prove the negative. Nothing in this section, clearly nothing requires it as mandatory. If the Defence has a section that indicates that it's mandatory, then they can provide it to the Court. But I'll have this ready -- it was sent for revision last week to CLSS and it should be available very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We are in the advantageous situation to have a specialist from the law in the courtroom. May we hear some observations on this issue by you, Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This law does not regulate the procedure in front of the courts. It's a law which regulates the procedure in front of the administrative bodies. And there is a law on - I don't know whether I'm able to translate it properly. It's a law on nonissue procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The English equivalent would be taking a deposition outside the court, or an ex parte hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with none of these. It's in front of the Court, but only it's nonissue procedure, so nothing is in issue in that procedure. It's taken by the judge with the parties present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you quote a source where we can find this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, we tried to locate that law during the weekend, but something was wrong with the electronic reading of Cyrillic in our computer. So we will try to obtain it this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I can assist counsel by giving him a copy just for his reference of the law we have for him to review. And while I agree that it's a procedure where, pretty much as Mr. Lukic stated, that the court, in other words, take a deposition of the person, there's no adverse party present. If you look at the articles in this law, it clearly indicates the court is involved. The first article in the procedure for declaring missing persons dead and proving death, the Court will decide on declaring missing persons dead and on the proof of death. And it goes on to describe the procedures that the Court has to go through in order to do that. And also sets the responsibility for the expenses for this procedure on the party seeking to have the declaration issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So as regards these legal facts, no doubt the burden of proof is with the OTP. But indeed, it could be helpful if we could obtain the necessary source, if not even the text, by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The articles seem to look proper, but the name of the law, I doubt that is properly translated. I will check this because this law is not meant to be used in front of the courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think this dispute can be settled between parties. And please, let the Chamber know during the hearing what is the result of your investigation as regards this law. Then may I ask, what about now the formal supplementary report on statistics provided by Madam Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The demographic report of Ms. Tabeau is, specifically the sections dealing with a statistical analysis of number of persons dead and missing in 1992 is now prepared and will be filed with the Defence and the Court today. We just received that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The progress evidently can't be stopped. Then what about the draft report from the in-house expert on the interrelationship between the documents allegedly having been signed by Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That is prepared. We're providing it today. We are providing it in English, and we rely upon the CLSS for the translation. It was just provided for the Defence on Friday, and we have it ready to distribute to the Chambers today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we ask the usher to distribute this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The Defence has a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, what would be the next exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit S295, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has not yet received an ERN number. So for purposes of record-keeping on future cases, could we provide it informally now or agree to substitute the ERNed copy when that is available.
